title: Data-Efficient Learning from Demonstration for Humanoid Robots via Feature-Level Perception and Prompt-Based Object Detection

statements: Data-Efficient Learning from Demonstration for Humanoid Robots via Feature-Level Perception and Prompt-Based Object Detection Keyhan Rayati∗ , AliReza Beigy∗ , Anoosheh Saadati∗ , Pourya Shahverdi† , Mehdi Tale Masouleh∗ , Ahmad Kalhor∗ , Wing-Yue Geoffrey Louie† arXiv:2610.26170v1 [cs.RO] 19 Oct 2026 ∗ Human and Robot Interaction Lab, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran Emails:
This paper introduces a data-efficient LfD framework for humanoid robots that learns manipulation skills from compact, task-specific features instead of raw images.

The proposed approach integrates layered visual preprocessing, Kinect-based human joint estimation, prompt-based object detection, and depth information to extract human motion features and three-dimensional object locations from demonstration videos.

experiments.summary: The experiments examine whether the proposed feature-level model can support humanoid imitation and manipulation from limited demonstrations.

evidence.quote: The experiments examine whether the proposed feature-level model can support humanoid imitation and manipulation from limited demonstrations.
Three scenarios are considered: upper-body imitation, pick-and-place, and object pushing.

limitations.summary: Kinect skeleton tracking may be inaccurate under occlusion or unusual arm positions, and detection failures can reduce the accuracy of the object state estimate.
items: Kinect skeleton tracking may be inaccurate under occlusion or unusual arm positions, and detection failures can reduce the accuracy of the object state estimate.
Removing the magnetic attachment would likely introduce additional grasping failures and requires a separate evaluation with a more realistic end-effector.

Future work should extend the framework to a wider range of manipulation skills, include task-level success in model selection, improve closed-loop correction during execution, and evaluate the method using more advanced sensors and dexterous end-effectors.
